props.title: A Few Good Men
props.initialSlug: A young JAG lawyer challenges military code of honor

sections.content: A Few Good Men (1992) stands as one of the greatest legal dramas ever made, powered by Aaron Sorkin's razor-sharp screenplay and Rob Reiner's precise direction. The film's climactic courtroom confrontation between Tom Cruise's Lt. Kaffee and Jack Nicholson's Col. Jessup ("You can't handle the truth!") became instantly iconic, but the whole film crackles with intelligent dialogue and mounting tension. Like The Verdict (1982) and 12 Angry Men (1957), it shows how courtroom drama can explore deeper questions about justice, honor, and moral responsibility.

sections.content: The military justice aspect of A Few Good Men connects to a proud lineage of films exploring the intersection of law and military culture. Paths of Glory (1957) showed Stanley Kubrick tackling military justice in WWI, while Rules of Engagement (2000) and The General's Daughter (1999) continued examining how military codes of conduct sometimes clash with civilian concepts of justice. These films share a fascination with how hierarchical military structures can both protect and corrupt notions of honor and duty.

The film's exploration of institutional power draws from classic whistleblower narratives like All the President's Men (1976) and anticipates later films like Spotlight (2015). In each case, determined investigators must pierce through layers of institutional protection to expose wrongdoing, often at great personal and professional risk. The theme of speaking truth to power resonates particularly strongly in A Few Good Men through its examination of military culture. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Legal Thriller

sections.content: A Few Good Men helped revitalize the legal thriller genre for the 1990s, paving the way for films like Primal Fear (1996) and The Firm (1993). What sets it apart is how it combines elements of military drama with courtroom proceedings, creating a unique hybrid that explores both legal strategy and military honor. The film's influence can be seen in later works like JAG (1995-2005) and even The Code (2019), which continue exploring the specialized world of military justice.
